principles:
**Shared requirement.** Architectural boundaries are enforced by a machine, not by review. Concretely: the composition root is reachable only from front ends and never from the core (F003); the core never depends on a front end (F004); front ends never depend on each other (F005); the core's own layers stay ordered (F006); no CLI or web framework enters the core, guarded both authoritatively and in a fast local tier (F008, F009); the permitted edges are declared in one readable artifact rather than inferred (F010); and the check runs at a defined place in the hook and CI pipeline (F116).

**Source and agreement level.** `py-launch-blueprint` at pin `b08bccfb` states the principle in its own words — `docs/adr/0017-hexagonal-core-and-boundary-enforcement.md`, "enforce the boundaries mechanically rather than by convention" — and realizes it in five `import-linter` contracts (`pyproject.toml:318-355`), a `tach.toml` module graph, and a subtree-scoped `ruff.toml` banned-api list (`src/py_launch_blueprint/core/ruff.toml:13`). `ts-launch-blueprint` at pin `cb1cbcb` has none of it; `docs/port/DIVERGENCE-ANALYSIS.md:77` records why — "ts's flat `src/` with one front-end and no core/front-end split leaves nothing for these tools to check (consequence of F001)". `DIVERGENCE-ANALYSIS.md:77-79,241` puts F003–F010 and F116 in one item-level bucket, cause class C, `harmonize: partly`; F020 is class C, `harmonize: no`; F021 is class G ("no precedent either side"), `harmonize: no`.

| Rows | What must agree | What may vary |
|---|---|---|
| F003, F004, F005, F007, F008 | **Policy and capability**: a violation must fail a build or a check, in every repository that has a core/front-end split | the mechanism entirely |
| F006, F009, F010, F116 | **Capability**: internal layering is constrained; a fast tier exists; the permitted edges are declared; the check has a defined tier | mechanism, granularity and tier, because they follow from how fast the ecosystem's authoritative check is |
| F020 | nothing above "the public name is unambiguous" | everything: Python needs an importable package directory, Node needs none, Rust namespaces by `Cargo.toml` `name` |
| F021 | — | Rust-only; no agreement to preserve |

No shared low-level value is recommended. There is no owner requirement for one, and the evidence does not support the same tradeoff in all three ecosystems: Python's checker exists because the language has no compile-time module direction, while Rust's compiler makes the same guarantee stronger and free at the crate edge. The one value worth naming across all three is the **declared-graph artifact** (F010) — py has `tach.toml`, rs gets `cargo metadata --no-deps` plus an assertion test, ts has nothing — and even there the agreement is at capability level, not a shared file format.

**The question the whole item turns on was settled by execution, not by argument.** A one-package crate with `pub mod core_layer;` and `pub(crate) mod cli_layer;`, where `core_layer.rs` contains `use crate::cli_layer::CliThing;` — core reaching upward into the front end, exactly what F004 forbids — **compiles clean** (check `A`, `review/evidence/r02-workspace-probe.log`). This is not a gap in the lints. The Rust Reference defines visibility as who may *name* an item, and `pub(crate)` grants naming rights to the entire crate, including the module that must not have them. For this requirement, module visibility points the wrong way.

On the crate edge the same four violations are build failures (checks `C1`–`C4`): `E0433` for the code tier and `error: cyclic package dependency` from Cargo's own resolution for the manifest tier, before rustc runs.

**Observable acceptance criteria.** Criteria 1–11 were executed in this run; 12–14 are requirements on a template that does not yet exist and are **not** results.

**Architectural alternatives compared, before any tool was weighed.**

| Alternative | Shape | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Single package, module visibility plus review** — the faithful F020 precedent | `src/core/`, `src/cli/`, `src/web/` with `pub(crate)` | **Rejected on executed evidence.** Check `A`: the violating code compiles. F007 fails outright and F003/F004/F005 with it. It is the ts position, which `DIVERGENCE-ANALYSIS.md:77` records as having no boundary tool at any tier |
| **B. Single package plus an intra-crate layer-contract linter** — the literal `import-linter`/`tach` port | a tool reading the module graph and failing on a forbidden edge | **Rejected on adoption and fit, not on absence.** A candidate exists and this run found it: `boundary` 0.27.0 (binary `boundary`, Rust analyzer `boundary-rust`). See the paragraph below |
| **C. Single package plus `cargo-deny` on the external graph only** | one package, ban frameworks nowhere in particular | **Rejected.** `bans` acts on packages; with one package there is no sub-package to confine a framework to. It can only say "this workspace may not use `axum`", which is false — the web surface must |
| **D. Multi-crate workspace, virtual manifest** — `jj`'s shape, binaries in `crates/cli` | `[workspace]` with no `[package]` | **Rejected on R49 and R69 compatibility; ranked second.** Identical enforcement, but the published package stops being the repository root, so R49's package-relative `include` allow-list and both `path` fields move, and R69's `[[bin]] required-features = ["web"]` moves to whichever package declares the feature |
| **E. Multi-crate workspace with a root package** | `[package] rs-launch-blueprint` + `[workspace] members = ["crates/*"]` | **Chosen.** The Cargo Book names the shape: "If the `[workspace]` section is added to a `Cargo.toml` that already defines a `[package]`, the package is the root package of the workspace." Every R49 field stays byte-identical |

**Alternative B deserves its own paragraph, because this synthesis corrects the Opus raw on it.** The Opus report's landscape says an intra-crate layer-contract checker "does not exist in maintained form" and rejects alternative B "for absence of a candidate". That is **falsified in its absolute form**. `boundary` exists on crates.io at **0.27.0**, published **2026-04-02**, licensed `MIT OR Apache-2.0`, with **30** published versions, and its README declares `[x] Rust language support`, a `.boundary.toml` carrying a `[layers]` glob contract, and a failing mode `boundary check <path> --fail-on error` (checks `EF1a`–`EF1l`, `review/evidence/r02-ecosystem-figures.log`; `GET https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/boundary`, `GET https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/boundary-rust/versions`, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebelopsio/boundary/main/README.md`, all retrieved 2026-09-17). What is true, and what actually decides the alternative, is its adoption and scope: `rebelopsio/boundary` carries **5** stars and **1** open issue, was last pushed **2026-04-02T20:17:15Z**, and 90-day downloads read **185** for `boundary` and **262** for `boundary-rust` on 2026-09-17. By the prompt's rubric it is **stable-quiet** — 5.5 months since its last release does not reach the six-month investigate trigger and no concrete at-risk signal was found — but its README records `[ ] Monorepo / multi-service support` as an **unchecked** roadmap item, and a Cargo workspace is precisely a multi-package repository. So alternative B is rejected because putting a template's architecture gate on a five-star tool whose multi-package support is an open roadmap box is disproportionate, and because a `boundary` exit code is still not a *build* error — not because nothing exists. It is a named **watch-not-adopt** candidate and a re-verify trigger.

**Why the chosen design preserves each principle.**

| Row | Preserved by | Tier | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| F003 composition-root isolation | `composition` is a module of the facade `[lib]`; `core`, `cli` and `web` do not depend on the facade | `cargo check` | check `C4` |
| F004 inward-only core | `crates/core/Cargo.toml` names no front end, and the reverse edge is a Cargo cycle | `cargo check` + Cargo resolution | checks `C1`, `C2` |
| F005 front-end independence | `crates/cli` and `crates/web` name only `core` | `cargo check` | check `C3` |
| F006 core internal layering | the production adapter moves **out** of `core` into the facade, so "adapters above services above models" becomes a crate edge; the models-below-services ordering inside `core` stays module privacy plus R04's private-`mod` root barrel. **This is the one row the split does not fully compile-enforce** — see `BASELINE-REVIEW: F006` | `cargo check` for the adapters edge; convention below it | check `C4`'s mechanism |
| F007 mechanical over conventional | every row above fails a build, not a review | — | checks `A`, `C1`–`C4` |
| F008 framework-bleed, authoritative | `cargo deny --all-features check bans` with `deny[].wrappers`; guards the *manifest*, the only remaining way a framework could reach `core` | pre-push + CI | checks `CD1a`–`CD4b` of the cargo-deny log |
| F009 framework-bleed, fast mirror | `crates/core/clippy.toml` scoped to one member, plus `cargo check`, which already rejects `use axum::…` in `core` | the edit loop | checks `D1`–`D3` |
| F010 declared graph | the member manifests are the declaration; a `cargo metadata --no-deps` assertion test pins the intended edge set | `cargo test` | check `F` |
| F020 namespacing | the package name *is* the namespace; flat `crates/<name>/src/` with no directory nesting | — | the five surveyed workspaces |
| F021 topology | this decision | — | `OVERRIDE (OV-03)` |

**F009's mechanism is not a translation of py's; a literal port was ruled out by execution.** py's fast tier works because `ruff` resolves configuration per directory subtree. Clippy does not. Three executed cases decide it: a `clippy.toml` at the **package root** of a single package flagged `src/core_layer.rs` *and* `src/cli_layer.rs`, so it cannot ban a framework in the core without banning it in the CLI (check `D1`); a `clippy.toml` at `src/clippy.toml`, py's nested shape, was **ignored** — zero `disallowed type` diagnostics on code that a package-root file flags, while the crate still compiled, so the zero is not a compile failure (check `D2`); and `crates/core/clippy.toml` under `cargo clippy --workspace` flagged only `crates/core/src/lib.rs` and left the identical use in `crates/cli/src/lib.rs` untouched (check `D3`). F009's capability is available in Rust at *package* granularity and nowhere else, which makes the split a second, independent reason for itself rather than a consequence of the F004 argument.

**F008's configuration, and the one entry that cannot be written.** The `deny.toml` `[bans]` section carries one `deny` entry per framework:

```toml
[bans]
multiple-versions = "warn"
deny = [
  { crate = "axum", wrappers = ["rs-launch-blueprint-web"], reason = "core and the CLI are framework-agnostic (F008)" },
  { crate = "clap", wrappers = ["rs-launch-blueprint-cli", "rs-launch-blueprint"], reason = "argument parsing belongs to the CLI layer and to the serve binary's required global core (F008)" },
]
```

`wrappers` is keyed on the **banned crate** and requires *every direct dependent* in the resolved graph to be listed. This run executed the consequence the Opus raw predicted from reading `src/bans.rs` but could not test: a `tokio` row confined to the web member **fails a clean tree**, because `axum` depends on `tokio` directly and is therefore a second unlisted direct parent (checks `CD4a`, `CD4b`). **`tokio` deliberately has no row.** The mechanism for every crate `wrappers` cannot express is the F010 test's second table — `crates/core`'s external-dependency **allow-list**, keyed on the *protected member* rather than on the banned crate, which handles `tokio` cleanly and also catches a framework nobody thought to ban. The two members are complementary, not redundant. The `clap` row carries two wrappers because R69 puts the `rslbp-serve` binary's required global core on the facade; it needs re-verification once R60's companion crates are known, since a direct dependent such as `clap_complete` must be added to the list or the row dropped.

**Two operational findings that no engine report carries, both executed here.** First, `--all-features` is a **global** flag: `cargo deny check bans --all-features` — the form the Opus and perplexity legs imply — is rejected by the argument parser with `unexpected argument '--all-features' found` (check `CD5a`). Second, and this is why the flag is not optional for this topology: without it the resolved graph holds only the three non-optional packages, and the optional `rs-launch-blueprint-web` member, `axum` and `tokio` are **absent from it entirely** (checks `CD5b`, `CD5c`, `CD5d`). A default-feature run would therefore be checking a graph in which the web surface does not exist. The invocation this decision recommends is `cargo deny --all-features check bans`, in that order.

**A third executed finding corrects a claim about the web feature's reach.** The Opus raw states that with `web` off "`cargo build` does not compile the web member at all (verified)". That is true of a *root-scoped* build (check `B1`) and false of a workspace-scoped one: `cargo build --workspace` with the feature off compiles `rs-launch-blueprint-web` regardless, because **workspace membership, not the root package's feature, decides which members are built** (check `B3`). The optional-dependency edge governs the facade's graph, not the workspace's build set. This matters to R11's job shape and to any hook or CI command written `--workspace`; it does not change the topology, and the feature-gated `rslbp-serve` binary is still skipped by a default build, as `required-features` specifies (check `B4`).

**Cross-repo adjudication.** Changes to py and ts are a follow-on project; this supplies their rationale. **py** is the reference realization and needs no change: its two-tier split is the right shape for a language whose authoritative check must build a whole import graph. **ts**'s absence is contingent drift rather than a missing capability — there is no core/front-end split for a boundary tool to guard, so the rows are vacuous rather than violated. It is not *justified* (no `D-0nn` records a decision) but it is not independently actionable either; if ts ever grows a second front end, the ecosystem's realizations are `eslint-plugin-boundaries` and `dependency-cruiser`, and the TypeScript compiler supplies no crate equivalent, so ts would land on py's tool-based tier, not Rust's. **rs** preserves the principle at a *stronger* level than either source, because Rust's enforcement is the build itself rather than a checker a contributor can skip. That is a justified ecosystem difference and needs no harmonization.

The capability py's two tiers exist to provide is preserved and the tiers are better than py's, because Rust's fast tier is the compiler. Whether the CI check is its own job or a step, and how it is path-skip-gated, is R11's `ci-job-structure` and is **not** decided here; membership of the aggregate required check is R12's; the `lefthook` wiring is R37's.

Pre-push rather than pre-commit is a deliberately conservative placement, and this run narrowed but did not close the measurement it turns on: one `cargo deny --all-features check bans` pass on the probe completed in **0.437 s** wall clock in the committed log (check `CD6`); every rerun records a different sub-second value, 0.475 s on the rerun performed for this decision. That probe is a six-package, path-only workspace with no registry crates resolved, so the figure is a **floor**, not a figure for the real template, whose resolved graph will hold hundreds of crates. It establishes that the tool is not seconds-slow on a small graph; it does not establish the real cost. Moving the manifest guard to pre-commit is the ranked runner-up and becomes the right answer once P03 measures it on both runners.
